research_text:
## 1. API and meaning of the finding

`java.security.MessageDigest` provides message-digest algorithms: it processes data and returns a fixed-length hash. The algorithm is selected by the string passed to `getInstance`. Thus, for a finding associated with a resolved `MessageDigest` factory call, **“found SHA-1” concerns the algorithm-selection argument**, not the digest bytes or their subsequent use. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

The supplied message lists six accepted spellings. The current CrySL file instead lists exactly three literals: `SHA-256`, `SHA-384`, and `SHA-512`. It does not explain the additional spellings in the detector message. The finding alone does not establish the digest’s purpose, an authentication requirement, or runtime reachability. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

## 2. Documented usage and security guidance

Oracle documents obtaining an instance for an algorithm, supplying data through `update`, and completing the computation with `digest`. `digest(byte[])` performs a final update itself before completing the computation; completion resets the digest object. Provider availability matters, and acquisition can throw `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

Oracle’s `MessageDigest` documentation supports SHA-1 as an API algorithm; it does **not** prescribe a general remediation for a SHA-1 finding. Separately, NIST recommends transitioning away from SHA-1 for cryptographic protection and identifies SHA-2 and SHA-3 as alternatives. Its guidance distinguishes new protection from handling previously protected information. NIST’s federal guidance is not the same thing as the CrySL rule’s three-name allow-list. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

A plain digest is not a keyed message authentication code. Oracle documents `javax.crypto.Mac` separately for integrity based on a shared secret. An equality comparison by itself does not establish that authentication is intended. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Mac.html))

## 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Stored and wire values:** SHA-1 produces 160 bits; SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 produce 256, 384, and 512 bits respectively. Changing the algorithm therefore changes the represented digest and may affect any format or protocol that specifies it. The `MessageDigest` documentation does not define an automatic conversion or a general migration path for existing identifiers, persisted values, or wire contracts. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Existing contracts:** NIST notes that backward compatibility and interoperability can require transition time, and that SHA-1 may remain necessary for handling information protected before its transition deadline. Neither source establishes a migration for a particular external contract. ([nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/CSWP/NIST.CSWP.39-upd1.pdf))
- **Platform support:** Java SE 8’s `MessageDigest` documentation requires SHA-256 but does not list SHA-384 or SHA-512 among its mandatory algorithms. Java SE 26 requires SHA-256 and SHA-384, but does not list SHA-512 among the mandatory algorithms. An explicitly selected provider can have different availability; consult the applicable release and provider documentation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

The appropriate compatibility evidence differs for a cache key, runtime discriminator, persisted identifier, and security digest. The supplied finding does not identify which applies.

## 4. Matching rule in the supplied CrySL source

The current file declares `SPEC java.security.MessageDigest` and contains this **verbatim factory matching clause and condition**:

```text
	g1: getInstance(algorithm);
	g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;
```

```text
	algorithm in {"SHA-256", "SHA-384", "SHA-512"};
```

The file declares `algorithm` as `java.lang.String`. The factory patterns constrain the **argument count** to one or two: the first argument is bound as `algorithm`, and the second is `_`. The file does not give that second argument a type in the clause. It also models `update` and `digest` events on the declared specification, with the argument shapes and bounds shown in the file. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

**A merely same-named method on an unrelated API is not explicitly named by this rule:** its specification is `java.security.MessageDigest`. However, the file itself does not define a scanner’s receiver or declaring-type resolution, so it cannot establish whether a particular scanner implementation could nevertheless match such a method. It also does not document how a scanner formats findings or handles unresolved arguments. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

## Source limitations

The CrySL URL points to a moving `master` branch. The detector’s bundled revision was not supplied, and the reported SHA-256 was not independently verified here. No application call trace, digest purpose, external contract, runtime, or provider was supplied.

- Oracle `MessageDigest`, Java SE 26: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html
- Oracle standard algorithm names: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html#messagedigest-algorithms
- Oracle `MessageDigest`, Java SE 8: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/MessageDigest.html

- NIST SHA-1 transition: https://csrc.nist.gov/news/2022/nist-transitioning-away-from-sha-1-for-all-apps
